plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates the U-Net architecture used as the noise-prediction backbone in a diffusion model. The diagram is organized as a symmetric encoder-decoder structure: the encoder path (left branch) shows a sequence of orange-shaded three-dimensional feature map volumes that progressively downsample the input from 256×256×3 through 256×256×128, 128×128×128, 64×64×256, 32×32×256, 16×16×512, down to 8×8×512 at the bottleneck, while the decoder path (right branch) shows dark steel-blue feature map volumes that mirror the encoder at each spatial scale as the resolution is progressively restored. The sizes of these volumes correspond to the input sizes; for example, the block for 256x256x3 has a large shape thins hape while 8x8x512 is long with a small surface. Four horizontal “Concatenate” arrows connect matching encoder and decoder blocks at four resolution levels, forming the characteristic skip connections of a U-Net. A small blue square node labeled “t” injects the diffusion timestep via a “time embedding” branch, with arrows feeding it into each processing block. Two block types are annotated in a legend at lower right: a plain “Res. block” (used at larger spatial scales) and a “Res. block + self-attention” (used at smaller spatial scales near the bottleneck). This figure demonstrates how a conditioned U-Net with residual blocks, skip connections, and time-step injection serves as the learned denoiser in a diffusion generative model.

interactions.label: Animate encoder-decoder pass
interactions.teaches: The U-Net first compresses spatial resolution while increasing channel depth, then restores resolution while reusing same-scale encoder features through concatenate skip connections

interactions.label: Diffusion timestep t
interactions.teaches: Every residual block receives the same global diffusion-time condition, so the denoiser changes its behavior depending on how noisy the current sample is
At the 16×16 resolution, self-attention lets each spatial position compare against all other positions, unlike a plain residual block that mainly mixes local neighborhoods

demo_steps.title: Start with the noisy image and time condition
demo_steps.narration: The noisy input image enters at 256×256 resolution. The timestep t is embedded once, then injected into every residual block along the bottom branch.

demo_steps.title: Encoder: downsample to compact features
demo_steps.narration: Step through the encoder levels from 256×256 down to 16×16. Each downsampling stage reduces spatial size while increasing or preserving channel capacity.

demo_steps.title: Bottleneck at 8×8×512
demo_steps.narration: The bottleneck has the smallest spatial grid but a large channel dimension. It carries the most compressed global representation before decoding begins.

demo_steps.title: Decoder: upsample and concatenate
demo_steps.narration: As the decoder restores resolution, matching encoder features are concatenated through the salmon skip arrows. The pulsing arrows show where fine-scale information re-enters the reconstruction path.

demo_steps.title: Inspect attention at 16×16
demo_steps.narration: Click the 16×16 self-attention block to open the overlay. The selected position attends over the full 16×16 grid, giving the network long-range context at a manageable spatial size.

demo_steps.title: Change the diffusion time
demo_steps.narration: Move t toward an early or late diffusion step. The e(t) badges update at every residual block, emphasizing that the same U-Net is conditioned differently throughout the denoising process.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use an oblique deep-learning-diagram style: each feature map is a rectangular front face with a short diagonal depth offset to the upper-right. Lay out the U shape along x from about -8 to +8 with all volumes resting on a common baseline y=0. Encode spatial size primarily as vertical height: 256→4.0 units, 128→2.0, 64→1.0, 32→0.55, 16→0.32, 8→0.22. Encode channel count primarily as horizontal face width: 3→0.12 units, 128→0.85, 256→1.25, 512→2.1, so the 8×8×512 bottleneck reads as a long low slab. Approximate encoder x positions: input image -7.8, 256 blocks -7.1 and -6.5, 128 block -5.6, 64 block -4.6, 32 block -3.6, 16 block -2.3, 8 bottleneck -0.9. Mirror decoder positions to +0.9, +2.3, +3.6, +4.6, +5.6, +6.5, output +7.8. Dominant colors: burnt orange blocks #873f24, light orange blocks #cf7d58, black outlines #111111, salmon skip arrows #d47d5d, concatenate text dark brown #7a351f, time embedding arrows #496b7c, pale blue injection markers #8fb3c7, legend text grey-blue #5f879d. Dimension labels should be black, italic/slanted, placed near their source volumes with thin arrow leaders. Timestep embedding may be displayed as e(t); for correctness use a sinusoidal embedding preview such as [sin(t/1000·2π), cos(t/1000·2π)] or a small normalized scalar badge t/1000 beside each injection arrow. Self-attention overlay formula: for N=16×16=256 positions, Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d))V; draw all-to-all rays faintly and emphasize one selected query position.
interactionPlan.notes: Render volumes with simple BufferGeometry or extruded rectangles using an oblique offset vector around (0.28, 0.18) screen/world units so the front faces remain true rectangles. Use generated noise textures for the input and output planes. Labels should be billboarded or rendered in a 2D overlay layer to stay readable. The passPhase state should trigger short tweened highlight animations: enc states glow the active block and show a downward/downsampling arrow between levels; dec states glow the active block and pulse the corresponding Concatenate skip line before fading. For timestep, update all e(t) badges and briefly brighten every blue injection arrow on slider change. For inspectAttentionBlock, make only the 16×16 self-attention volumes clickable; clicking opens a semi-transparent inset overlay without moving the architecture, with a close-on-click-away behavior.
